title: Map your pattern first
teaches: Before you fix a trading mistake, map it: write down what came before, during and after it the same day, name it plainly, tell a mistake (breaking your plan) from a loss, and find the one that repeats.

facts.quote: Behavioral finance holds that investors tend to fall into predictable patterns of destructive behavior. In other words, they make the same mistakes repeatedly.
facts.claim: Investors tend to fall into predictable patterns and make the same mistakes over and over.

facts.quote: selling winning positions and holding onto losing positions (disposition effect)
facts.claim: Selling winners and holding losers is a common, named pattern: the disposition effect.

facts.quote: Kahneman uses prospect theory to highlight biases of judgment—overconfidence, optimism, hindsight, and overreaction to past events
facts.claim: Kahneman's work lists hindsight among investors' biases of judgment.

facts.quote: These errors and biases lead to poor investment decisions.
facts.claim: Those biases lead to poor investment decisions.

facts.quote: The good news is that your emotional reactions happen again and again for the same reason. There’s no randomness in the mental game.
facts.claim: Your emotional reactions repeat for the same reasons; they are not random.

facts.quote: To begin mapping your pattern, keep a record of what happens before, during, and after your trading mistakes.
facts.claim: Mapping starts with a record of what happens before, during and after each mistake.

facts.quote: Look closely at the specific emotions, thoughts, actions, and decisions that are automatically triggered. They are the data that will help you understand the cause of the problem.
facts.claim: The emotions, thoughts, actions and decisions around a mistake are the data that explain it.

facts.quote: If all you do is beat yourself up for having these problems or losing money because of them, you will just feel bad and make the situation worse.
facts.claim: Beating yourself up over a mistake only makes things worse.

facts.quote: By choosing to blow off steam, or trying to forget what happened and move on, they are essentially deleting the missing pieces that can ultimately help them prevent future bombs from going off.
facts.claim: Forgetting a mistake and moving on throws away the clues that could prevent the next one.

facts.quote: Instead, you want to write the clues down and create a detailed map of your reactions.
facts.claim: Write the clues down and build a detailed map of your reactions.

facts.quote: consider setting an alarm at some regular frequency that isn’t too disruptive (i.e., every 15, 30, or 60 minutes) to take stock of where you are.
facts.claim: Tendler suggests an alarm every 15, 30 or 60 minutes to check where you are emotionally.

facts.quote: Fear is why you get out of a trade too early, greed is why you jump in too soon, anger is why you revenge trade.
facts.claim: Fear drives early exits, greed drives early entries, and anger drives revenge trades.

facts.quote: I’m hyper-focused on one position and constantly looking at PnL
facts.claim: In Tendler's sample map, the behavior is fixating on one position and the P&L.

facts.quote: I’m focused on getting revenge and getting my money back
facts.claim: In the same map, the trader's decisions turn to revenge and getting the money back.

facts.quote: I’m taking the same trade over and over, until it’s clear I’m wrong and getting nowhere
facts.claim: In the same map, the trading mistake is taking the same trade over and over.

facts.quote: I can’t believe this is happening. I’m not letting the market stop me
facts.claim: In the same map, the thought is: I'm not letting the market stop me.

facts.quote: You’ll first look to tighten your technical skills by analyzing your trades, tightening your rules, and learning new techniques. That’s the correct first step.
facts.claim: Tightening your skills and your rules is the right first step.

facts.quote: But when the bleeding continues, that’s proof the answer won’t come from that side of the game.
facts.claim: If the mistakes keep costing you after that, the answer isn't technical.

facts.quote: When these mistakes occur repeatedly, and at times when you can’t stop yourself from making them, your emotions are the reason.
facts.claim: A mistake you repeat and can't stop yourself from making is driven by emotion.

facts.quote: So you immediately re-enter losing trades out of anger and FOMO positions other traders are in even though they are outside your system.
facts.claim: Two named mistakes: re-entering losers out of anger, and FOMO into trades outside your system.

facts.quote: You also need a detailed map of what those emotional reactions look like at a micro level, so that in real time you can quickly spot them and minimize the damage.
facts.claim: A detailed map lets you spot the reaction in real time and limit the damage.

facts.quote: Emotions are not the problem. They are signals, pointing you in the direction of where the real problem lies.
facts.claim: Emotions are signals that point to the real problem; they are not the problem.

facts.quote: You need to create a fact-based account of when and how your emotional volatility shows up. Over time you will be able to recognize a pattern and then you can work to disrupt how that pattern plays out.
facts.claim: Mapping is a fact-based record of when and how your emotions swing, so you can see the pattern and break it.

facts.quote: In my system are three distinct stages and each stage has its own set of steps and strategies. The big picture is: Map Your Pattern
facts.claim: Tendler's system has three stages, and the first is Map Your Pattern.

facts.quote: Identify the Roots of Your Problem: Here you dig deeper to find the hidden flaws, biases, illusions, and errors in learning that are the real cause of your problems.
facts.claim: Stage two digs for the hidden flaws and biases behind the problem.

facts.quote: Correct Your Problem: This is about consistently and relentlessly working to correct the problems as they appear day-to-day.
facts.claim: Stage three is correcting the problem, day after day.

facts.quote: Advice focused on controlling your emotions relies on the premise that you must keep holding ideas in your mind to control and fight against greed, anger or fear. I consider this to be a “band-aid” on the problem.
facts.claim: Fighting an emotion in the moment is a band-aid, not a fix.

facts.quote: You stop trading on days your emotions are too high, until you can get your head on straight.
facts.claim: Sitting out the days your emotions run high is one of the work-arounds Tendler describes.

facts.quote: Yes, they can be good short-term strategies, but they’re best used like training wheels.
facts.claim: Work-arounds help in the short term, but they are training wheels, not the fix.

facts.quote: When you spend time pretending the emotion isn’t there, rationalizing it away, or writing it off as a one-time event, you are not actually solving the problem. You are just managing it.
facts.claim: Ignoring an emotion or calling it a one-off manages the problem; it doesn't solve it.

facts.quote: Win and you’ll end up right back in this spot again because you’ve taught yourself that when things get difficult, abandoning your process can save you.
facts.claim: When things get hard, a win after you abandon your process teaches you to abandon it again.

facts.quote: getting rewarded for bad behavior temporarily validates the fantasy
facts.claim: Getting paid for bad behavior makes it feel right, for a while.

facts.quote: You’ll see traders make mistakes like not letting a winner run to avoid the risk of it going against them
facts.claim: Not letting a winner run, for fear it turns against you, is a common mistake.

facts.quote: a great way to build that self-awareness is to take our "emotional temperature" every hour during the trading day.
facts.claim: Check your emotional temperature every hour while you trade.

facts.quote: Identifying how you're feeling is the first step in shifting our mindsets
facts.claim: Naming how you feel is the first step to changing your state.

facts.quote: Every journal entry needs to finish with action steps: a checklist of essential to-do items for the coming trading session
facts.claim: Each journal entry should end with action steps for the next session.

facts.quote: It's not enough to simply say, "I'm going to work on better entries". You need to elaborate how, specifically, you're going to improve your entry execution.
facts.claim: A vague goal isn't enough; spell out exactly how you'll improve.

facts.quote: This is why very accomplished traders I've known and worked with record their journals after the market close
facts.claim: Accomplished traders Steenbarger has worked with record their journal after the close.

facts.quote: This is why it's important that your daily trading journal include highlights from the day of what you did well (that you want to continue and expand) and what you didn't do well (that you want to improve).
facts.claim: Your daily journal should log what you did well and what you didn't.

facts.quote: We often hear that trading success is 80 (or 90!) percent psychology. This is not even vaguely credible.
facts.claim: Steenbarger rejects the claim that trading success is 80 or 90 percent psychology.

facts.quote: Too often, traders try to make money in markets before they've gone through the mastery process
facts.claim: Many traders put money at risk before they have mastered their method.

facts.quote: But fear and greed are not the issues. The issue is attempting to short circuit the process of mastering markets.
facts.claim: Fear and greed are not the root issue; skipping the work of mastering markets is.

facts.quote: Notice that the goal is not to replace negative emotions with positive ones. The goal is to replace emotional distraction with intensive focus.
facts.claim: The goal isn't swapping bad feelings for good ones; it's replacing distraction with focus.

facts.quote: A wise reader pointed out that journaling might be necessary to shape our self-coaching, but it is not sufficient.
facts.claim: Journaling alone is not enough (a reader's point that Steenbarger calls wise and builds on).

facts.quote: If we're overcome with frustration when we fall short of desired results, that frustration impacts our focus and our motivation. Instead of doubling down on our efforts at improvement, we get down on ourselves and distract ourselves from those efforts.
facts.claim: Getting down on yourself pulls your effort away from improving.

facts.quote: when we review only the things we do wrong--the result is a negative environment for our development.
facts.claim: Reviewing only your mistakes makes a negative environment for growth.

facts.quote: The best practice here is not just to rehearse our best trading, but to become intimately familiar with all the things we do wrong so that we can catch them in real time
facts.claim: Know your own mistakes well enough to catch them in real time.

facts.quote: Hindsight bias is the tendency to believe past events were easier to predict after they've already happened.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias: after the fact, events seem easier to predict than they were.

facts.quote: Keeping an investment journal helps investors remember their initial assumptions and avoid falling prey to hindsight bias.
facts.claim: A journal keeps your original reasons, which guards against hindsight bias.

facts.quote: Analyzing the results of your decisions will help you understand what went right or wrong and help you identify other solutions or opportunities.
facts.claim: Reviewing your decisions shows what went right and what went wrong.

facts.quote: Outcome bias is the tendency to judge a decision by its result rather than the reasoning behind it, putting too much weight on how things turned out.
facts.claim: Outcome bias is judging a decision by how it turned out instead of by its reasoning.

facts.quote: This focus on outcomes can mislead investors, gamblers, and businesses into repeating risky choices or overlooking good ones.
facts.claim: Judging by outcomes leads people to repeat risky choices and overlook good ones.

facts.quote: Examining your past investment decisions is also telling—look for recurring mistakes or emotional triggers.
facts.claim: Go back over your past decisions and look for recurring mistakes and emotional triggers.

facts.quote: Schedule quarterly reviews focused on whether you’re adhering to your plan, not on market performance.
facts.claim: Review whether you followed your plan, not how the market did.

facts.quote: Once you’re aware of your tendencies, you’ll want to work on a concrete plan.
facts.claim: Once you know your tendencies, make a concrete plan to deal with them.

facts.quote: Pay attention to your emotional reactions during significant market moves.
facts.claim: Notice your emotional reactions when the market moves.

facts.quote: investors seem to have a knack for piling into investments at market tops and selling at the bottoms, whether due to fear of missing out (FOMO) or fear generally.
facts.claim: Fear of missing out (FOMO) pulls people into buying near the top.

facts.quote: Experiencing losses in the markets can be painful, but they are also almost always inevitable.
facts.claim: Losses in the market are painful but almost always inevitable.

facts.quote: Assess what went wrong carefully and objectively. If the cause was out of your hands, there is nothing that can be done. If you identify mistakes or missteps, take responsibility and learn from them.
facts.claim: After a loss, sort what was out of your hands from the mistakes that were yours to learn from.

facts.quote: Losses are common and a part of the risk.
facts.claim: Losses are common and part of the risk.

facts.quote: If you find yourself getting swept up in excitement or fear of missing out (FOMO) due to investment-related social media content, it’s best to pause and evaluate.
facts.claim: When excitement or FOMO from what everyone is posting pulls at you, pause and evaluate.

facts.quote: It is not uncommon for those facing a big loss to try to blame it on someone or something else rather than taking responsibility for their own poor decisions or excessive risk-taking.
facts.claim: After a big loss, people often blame someone or something else instead of owning their decisions.

facts.quote: Traders often fail when they let emotions like fear, greed, overconfidence, and herding behavior take over. This can lead to overtrading, trend-chasing, and scrambling to make up losses.
facts.claim: Fear, greed and overconfidence lead to overtrading, chasing and scrambling to make losses back.

facts.quote: The plan is written and must be followed and unaltered unless it's found not to work or the trader finds a way to improve it.
facts.claim: A trading plan is written down and followed; you change it only when it doesn't work or you find a better way.

facts.quote: A tactical trader should come up with rules for exactly when they will enter a trade.
facts.claim: A trading plan spells out exactly when you enter.

facts.quote: Plans shouldn't change whenever there's a loss or a rough patch.
facts.claim: A loss or a rough patch is not a reason to change the plan.

facts.quote: Trading plans should only be altered if a better way of trading or investing is uncovered.
facts.claim: Change the plan only when you have found a better way.

facts.quote: Understanding these psychological blind spots is the first step toward making smarter investment choices and avoiding costly mistakes.
facts.claim: Understanding your blind spots is the first step to avoiding costly mistakes.

facts.quote: Pausing before taking action is good advice, but according to Kahneman, awareness alone usually isn’t enough to overcome our biases.
facts.claim: Knowing about a bias usually isn't enough to overcome it.

facts.quote: Investors are found to systematically hold on to losing investments longer than rational expectations would predict, and they also sell winners too early.
facts.claim: Investors hold losers too long and sell winners too early.

facts.quote: Rather than locking in a paper loss, investors holding losing positions may even double down and take on greater risk in hopes of breaking even.
facts.claim: Rather than take a loss, people double down and take more risk to get back to even.

facts.quote: Hindsight bias occurs when people feel that they “knew it all along,” that is, when they believe that an event is more predictable after it becomes known than it was before it became known.
facts.claim: Hindsight bias is the 'knew it all along' feeling: once an event is known, it seems more predictable than it was before.

walkthroughs.title: Map before you fix
steps: A research review done for the SEC says investors make the same mistakes over and over. Yours repeat too.
Jared Tendler, who wrote The Mental Game of Trading, works in three stages: map your pattern, find the root, then correct it.
Mapping comes first. It's a fact-based record of when and how your emotions swing, so the pattern shows.

walkthroughs.title: What goes on the map
steps: When a mistake happens, write down what came before it, during it and after it.
Your thoughts, your feelings, what you did and how your decisions changed. Then name the mistake plainly.
Be a detective, not a critic. Beating yourself up just makes it worse.

walkthroughs.title: A loss is not a mistake
steps: A planned trade that hits its stop is a loss. Losses are part of the risk.
A mistake is breaking your own plan. It counts even when the trade makes money.
So judge the decision, not the result. Your review checks one thing first: whether you followed your plan.

questions.q: Your trading mistakes are mostly random, so there's no pattern worth mapping.
questions.why: False. A research review done for the SEC says investors make the same mistakes repeatedly. Tendler puts it plainly: there's no randomness in the mental game.
questions.lesson_line: Your mistakes repeat for a reason. What repeats can be mapped.

questions.q: You keep making the same costly mistake, even though you know the rule. What do you need before you can fix it?
choices: A record of when and why it happens
More willpower in the moment
A week away from the screens
A new setup to trade
questions.answer: A record of when and why it happens
questions.why: A record of when and why it happens. Tendler's first stage is a fact-based account of when and how your emotions swing. Investopedia calls understanding your blind spots the first step.
questions.lesson_line: Map it first. Then fix it.

wrong.More willpower in the moment: Fighting the urge in the moment is what Tendler calls a band-aid. It hasn't stopped this mistake so far.
wrong.A week away from the screens: A break can help short term, but Tendler calls work-arounds like that training wheels. You come back with the same blind spot.
wrong.A new setup to trade: The setup isn't the problem. You know the rule and break it anyway, so the habit comes with you to the next setup.

questions.q: When should you write down a trading mistake?
choices: The same day, while it's fresh
At month-end, all at once
Only when it costs a lot
Never, just forget it and move on
questions.answer: The same day, while it's fresh
questions.why: The same day. Coach Brett Steenbarger notes that accomplished traders record their journal after the close. A note written then still holds what you really thought.
questions.lesson_line: Write it down today, while you still remember why you clicked.

wrong.At month-end, all at once: By then you know how the trades ended, and that colors what you remember. A journal written at the time keeps your first reasons.
wrong.Only when it costs a lot: Small mistakes repeat and add up. Leave them out and your map has holes.
wrong.Never, just forget it and move on: Tendler says forgetting and moving on deletes the clues that could stop the next one.

questions.q: Once you know how a trade ended, it's easy to believe you saw it coming.
questions.why: True. That's hindsight bias, one of the biases of judgment in Kahneman's work. A journal written at the time shows what you really expected.
questions.lesson_line: Write down why you took the trade before you know how it ends.

questions.q: Fill in the word.
questions.sentence: A planned trade that hits its stop is a loss. Breaking your own plan is a ___.
questions.why: Mistake. Losses come with trading, and one loss is no reason to change the plan. A mistake is not doing what your plan says, and that's what you tag in your log.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are part of the risk. Breaking the plan is the mistake.

questions.q: A good review looks at what you did well, not only at your mistakes.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger's daily journal logs what you did well and what you didn't. Reviewing only mistakes, he says, makes a negative environment for growth.
questions.lesson_line: Log what you did well too. That's what you want to repeat on purpose.

questions.q: Being hard on yourself after a mistake helps you stop repeating it.
questions.why: False. Tendler says beating yourself up just makes the situation worse. Steenbarger agrees: getting down on yourself pulls effort away from improving. Own the mistake, then get curious about it.
questions.lesson_line: Be a detective, not a critic. Curious beats harsh.

questions.story: Your journal note on a losing trade reads: 'Down $400. Bad day.'
questions.q: What would make this note useful for finding your pattern?
choices: Your thoughts and feelings then
Who or what is to blame for it
The exact loss, down to the cent
A promise to do better tomorrow
questions.why: What you thought and felt before buying. Tendler maps the thoughts, emotions and decisions around a mistake, because that's the part that repeats. The dollar figure tells you what happened, not why.
questions.lesson_line: The P&L says what happened. Your thoughts and feelings say why.

wrong.Who or what is to blame for it: Blaming someone or something else skips your own part in it. Investopedia lists that as projection, an unhealthy way to cope.
wrong.The exact loss, down to the cent: You already have the number. What's missing is the why.
wrong.A promise to do better tomorrow: Steenbarger says a vague goal isn't enough. Spell out how you'll do it.

questions.q: Of your 8 plan breaks this month, 6 were the same mistake. What percent of your breaks was that one mistake?
questions.why: 75%. Six of your eight breaks were one mistake. That's your pattern, and it's where the map starts.
questions.lesson_line: Name each mistake the same way every time. Then the one that repeats stands out.

questions.story: You have no setup on your list today. A stock you don't follow is up 12%, and everyone online is talking about it. You buy it.
questions.q: Which tag fits this trade?
choices: FOMO, a trade outside your plan
Revenge, making back a loss
Hesitation, waiting too long
Cut a winner short
questions.answer: FOMO, a trade outside your plan
questions.why: FOMO, a trade outside your plan. Tendler names this mistake: jumping into positions other traders are in, even though they're outside your system. FINRA's advice when social media stirs up fear of missing out: pause and evaluate.
questions.lesson_line: Not on your list, not your trade. Tag it FOMO and note what pulled you in.

wrong.Revenge, making back a loss: There's no loss before this trade. Revenge comes after a loss.
wrong.Hesitation, waiting too long: The opposite. You jumped in fast.
wrong.Cut a winner short: That's an exit mistake. This one happened at the entry.

questions.story: Your plan is to hold while the trend holds. The stock is up 8% in three days. Scared to give it back, you sell it all.
questions.q: Which mistake do you log?
choices: Cut a winner short
Took profits by plan
Moved the stop
Chased the entry
questions.why: Cut a winner short. Your plan said hold, and fear made the call. Selling winners too early is one of the patterns research on investors keeps finding.
questions.lesson_line: Selling into strength is fine when the plan says so. Selling out of fear is the mistake.

wrong.Took profits by plan: Your plan said hold while the trend holds. You sold because you were scared, not because of a rule.
wrong.Moved the stop: No stop moved here. You sold the whole position.
wrong.Chased the entry: Nothing in the story is about the entry. The mistake was the exit.

questions.q: You only notice your frustration after the damage is done. What helps you catch it sooner?
choices: Check how you feel at set times
Watch your P&L more closely
Trade only on days you feel calm
Push the feelings aside and focus
questions.answer: Check how you feel at set times
questions.why: Check how you feel at set times. Tendler suggests an alarm every 15, 30 or 60 minutes. Steenbarger suggests taking your emotional temperature every hour.
questions.lesson_line: Check in on a timer, so you catch the build-up before it costs you.

wrong.Watch your P&L more closely: In Tendler's sample map, staring at the P&L is part of the problem, not the cure.
wrong.Trade only on days you feel calm: Sitting out the hot days is a work-around Tendler calls training wheels. You still won't see the build-up.
wrong.Push the feelings aside and focus: That hides the build-up you're trying to catch. Steenbarger says naming how you feel is the first step.

questions.story: This month's log: five chased entries lost $240, $180, $300, $220 and $260. Two stops you moved lower lost $450 and $500.
questions.q: Which mistake cost you more this month?
choices: Chasing, $1,200 in all
Moving the stop, the bigger hits
Neither, losses are part of trading
questions.why: Chasing, $1,200 in all. The two stop moves were the biggest single losses. Added up, the five chases cost more this month.
questions.lesson_line: Add up each mistake by name. The totals show where the money really went.

wrong.Moving the stop, the bigger hits: Each stop move hurt more, at $450 and $500. Added up, the five chases still cost more.
wrong.Neither, losses are part of trading: A planned stop-out is a loss. Chasing and moving a stop break the plan, so they're mistakes.

questions.q: Once you know which bias trips you up, that alone usually stops it.
questions.why: False. Investopedia notes Kahneman's view that awareness alone usually isn't enough. Steenbarger passes on a point from a reader he calls wise: journaling is necessary but not sufficient.
questions.lesson_line: The map shows you the problem. Fixing it takes a concrete plan.

questions.q: Today's journal entry ends with one line: 'Be more disciplined.' What would make it useful?
choices: One specific step for the next session
A longer list of what went wrong
A bigger profit goal for tomorrow
A harsher note to yourself
questions.answer: One specific step for the next session
questions.why: One specific step for the next session. Steenbarger says every journal entry should finish with action steps, and a vague goal isn't enough. Spell out how.
questions.lesson_line: End every journal entry with one specific thing to do differently next session.

wrong.A longer list of what went wrong: More problems with no plan changes nothing. Steenbarger warns that reviewing only mistakes makes a negative environment.
wrong.A bigger profit goal for tomorrow: That's a result, not a behavior. Your review checks whether you followed your plan.
wrong.A harsher note to yourself: Tendler says beating yourself up makes it worse. Be specific instead.

questions.story: Your plan says buy only on a pullback. Instead you chase a stock up 6% at the open. It closes up 10%, and you're green.
questions.q: How do you log this trade?
choices: A mistake, even though it paid
A good trade, since it worked
A new setup worth adding
No entry, it's a winner
questions.answer: A mistake, even though it paid
questions.why: A mistake, even though it paid. You broke your plan and got rewarded. Tendler warns that getting rewarded for bad behavior makes it feel right, for a while.
questions.lesson_line: A broken rule that pays still goes in the log as a mistake.

wrong.A good trade, since it worked: Judging a trade by its result is outcome bias. It leads you to repeat risky choices.
wrong.A new setup worth adding: One win off a broken rule proves nothing. Change the plan only when you've found a better way.
wrong.No entry, it's a winner: Winners go in the log too, and so do the rules you broke to get them.

questions.story: Tendler gives a sample map. Thought: 'I'm not letting the market stop me.' Behavior: glued to one position and the P&L. Decision: get the money back.
questions.q: What trading mistake does this map lead to?
choices: Taking the same losing trade again
Hesitating on a good entry
Selling a winner too early
Buying a stock everyone's chasing
questions.answer: Taking the same losing trade again
questions.why: Taking the same losing trade again. In Tendler's map, the mistake is taking the same trade over and over. The feeling underneath is revenge.
questions.lesson_line: The mistake comes last. Learn the thoughts that come first, and you can catch it sooner.

wrong.Hesitating on a good entry: This trader is pushing, not holding back. Hesitating comes from fear.
wrong.Selling a winner too early: There's no winner here. The trade already lost, and the trader wants the money back.
wrong.Buying a stock everyone's chasing: The focus is one position the trader already lost on, not a new hot name.

questions.story: You keep buying stocks after big run-ups, and most of those trades lose. Your written plan never says where an entry should be.
questions.q: What do you fix first?
choices: Write an entry rule into the plan
Work on your fear of missing out
Cut your size in half for now
Take a month off from trading
questions.answer: Write an entry rule into the plan
questions.why: Write an entry rule into the plan. Tendler calls tightening your rules the correct first step. You can't break a rule you don't have.
questions.lesson_line: Write the rule first. Then you can tell a gap in your plan from an emotional pattern.

wrong.Work on your fear of missing out: Maybe later. Tendler says you tighten the rules first, then look at the mental side if the mistakes keep coming.
wrong.Cut your size in half for now: Smaller size can limit the damage, but it fixes nothing. The gap in your plan is still there.
wrong.Take a month off from trading: You'd come back with the same gap in your plan.

questions.story: Your entry rule is written down and you know it cold. Still, about once a week you buy far above your entry point, usually after missing a few big moves.
questions.q: What does that tell you?
choices: It's an emotional pattern to map
The rule needs to be stricter
The entry rule doesn't work
It's bad luck, it will pass
questions.answer: It's an emotional pattern to map
questions.why: It's an emotional pattern to map. You know the rule and still break it. Tendler: when a mistake repeats and you can't stop yourself, emotions are the reason.
questions.lesson_line: Knowing the rule and breaking it anyway is the signal. Map what comes right before it.

wrong.The rule needs to be stricter: You already break a clear rule. Tendler: when the bleeding continues, the answer won't come from the technical side.
wrong.The entry rule doesn't work: You can't judge a rule you aren't following. Change the plan only when it's found not to work.
wrong.It's bad luck, it will pass: Tendler: there's no randomness in the mental game. This one shows up after missed moves, so it has a trigger.

questions.q: Fear, greed and anger are the real problem, not signals of a deeper one.
questions.why: False. Tendler: emotions are not the problem; they're signals pointing to where the real problem lies. Steenbarger agrees that fear and greed are not the issue.
questions.lesson_line: An emotion is a messenger. Read the message instead of just trying to silence it.

conflicts: Unit row vs the contract: docs/study/UNITS-foundations.md asks for 'the Five Leaks' (from the curriculum dossier) and 'the 17 mistake tags and 15 emotion tags'. The dossier is docs/curriculum, never a source, and the tag lists live in app code (api/services/journal_two/tag_suggest.py), not on an owner-ruling page, so neither is taught or quizzed. The unit names mistakes the way Tendler, the SEC-hosted report and Investopedia name them (FOMO, revenge, cutting a winner, chasing, moving a stop). If the owner wants the Journal's own tag list taught, it needs his ruling first.

Writing from memory: Tendler (s2) says 'think back to previous instances where the errors happened, and start writing out those details as best you can', i.e. old mistakes from memory are a fine start. Investopedia (s9) and the SEC-hosted report (s1) warn that hindsight bends memory. No real disagreement: the file keys 'write a NEW mistake down the same day' (q03, q04) and never says old ones can't be noted.

Check-in timing: Tendler suggests an alarm 'every 15, 30, or 60 minutes'; Steenbarger suggests taking 'our emotional temperature' every hour (general advice, not his own habit; the checker fixed q12's why to say so). q12 keys 'at set times' and quotes both, never one interval as the rule.

Skill vs mental game: Tendler (s3) says tightening skills and rules is 'the correct first step' and the mental game is the answer only 'when the bleeding continues'; Steenbarger (s7) says trading being 80 or 90 percent psychology 'is not even vaguely credible' and that traders often risk money before mastering a method. They agree. q18 (no entry rule yet: fix the plan) and q19 (the rule is known and still broken: map the emotion) are keyed on that split.

Awareness vs mapping: Investopedia (s15) gives Kahneman's view that 'awareness alone usually isn't enough'; Tendler makes mapping only stage one of three. Consistent; q14 keys 'knowing is not enough' and q02 keys 'map first', never 'map only'.
Steenbarger f61 ('journaling might be necessary ... but it is not sufficient') is a reader's point he calls wise and builds on; q14's why attributes it that way rather than as his own words.

Investopedia 'How to Avoid Emotional Investing' (s11) is written for long-term investors (quarterly reviews, dollar-cost averaging).
